current_criteria.name: visual_coherence
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer’s explicit spatial relationship claims — defined as assertions using terms like 'left of', 'behind', 'in front of', 'overlapping', 'centered relative to', 'slightly closer', 'relatively far apart', 'on', 'under', 'above', 'beneath', 'beside', or 'within' — are factually consistent with the visual layout and relative positioning of at least two visually confirmed objects in the image. It is ONLY applicable when: (1) both candidate answers pass multimodal_alignment (i.e., all object claims are visually grounded and factually correct), and (2) both answers contain at least one spatial claim. If either answer fails multimodal_alignment, visual_coherence is INAPPLICABLE — the worker must NOT evaluate or reference this criterion — and preference is assigned directly by multimodal_alignment disqualification (i.e., the multimodal-aligned answer is preferred). If neither answer contains a spatial claim, visual_coherence is INAPPLICABLE — preference must be determined by other criteria — and the worker must NOT assume or introduce any tiebreaker. When both answers pass multimodal_alignment and both contain spatial claims, visual_coherence is used as a tiebreaker — preference is given to the answer with fewer or no factual misrepresentations of spatial relationships — but only if the claims are explicitly and visually verifiable. Spatial claims must not be hallucinated or misidentified — such claims are disqualifying under multimodal_alignment, not under visual_coherence. Visual_coherence does NOT evaluate: (1) object identity, presence, or count (handled by visual grounding), (2) factual accuracy of attributes (handled by multimodal_alignment), (3) aesthetic or compositional terms (e.g., ‘balanced’, ‘harmonious’), (4) semantic or contextual inferences (e.g., ‘formal setting’, ‘indoor’), (5) motion trajectories (handled by action_or_state_accuracy), or (6) relative size or proportion (e.g., ‘small portion’, ‘most of the space’) — those are not spatial relationships. Workers must evaluate multimodal_alignment first — if one fails, visual_coherence is not considered — and preference is assigned directly by multimodal_alignment. Workers must never assume or introduce tiebreakers — especially arbitrary ones — when visual_coherence is inapplicable. If both answers are inapplicable (e.g., neither contains a spatial claim), preference must not be assigned — the pair should be marked as a tie or deferred to other criteria — without defaulting to a tiebreaker. Visual_coherence is strictly a tiebreaker — never a default preference tool — and must never be used to justify disqualification or preference for hallucinated or misidentified claims. Spatial claims are irrelevant if the answer is factually wrong — and must be evaluated only after visual grounding and multimodal_alignment are verified. The worker must not evaluate or reason about visual_coherence if either answer fails multimodal_alignment — and must immediately defer to multimodal_alignment or other criteria — without any ambiguity or room for interpretation. If both answers are invalid (e.g., both hallucinated), preference must not be assigned — the pair should be marked as a tie or deferred to other criteria — and workers must never assume or introduce tiebreakers. Finally, the criterion must explicitly state: (a) visual_coherence is never used to assign preference when one candidate fails multimodal_alignment — preference is determined solely by multimodal_alignment, (b) it is only a tiebreaker between two equally multimodal-aligned answers with spatial claims, (c) it is never used to justify preference for an invalid candidate, (d) spatial claims are mandatory for evaluation — no claim about visual representation (e.g., ‘smoke rising’) is evaluated under visual_coherence unless it is a spatial claim, (e) spatial accuracy is only evaluated if both candidates are multimodal-aligned — and (f) if neither candidate contains a spatial claim, preference must not be assigned — the pair must be marked as a tie or deferred to other criteria — without defaulting to a tiebreaker.

current_criteria.name: visual_ambiguity_resolution
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates how an answer handles *genuine visual ambiguities* — defined as objectively verifiable conditions where visual evidence is unclear due to occlusion, low resolution, shadow, motion blur, or partial visibility — without fabricating, hallucinating, or misrepresenting visual content. It applies ONLY when: (1) the visual evidence is objectively ambiguous (verified by worker against image features like occlusion, blur, shadow, or partial visibility), and (2) the answer makes a visual claim directly affected by that ambiguity. If either condition is not met, the criterion is INAPPLICABLE — preference must be determined by visual_grounding or multimodal_alignment first. The criterion is strictly a tiebreaker — it is NEVER invoked if one candidate is disqualified under visual_grounding or multimodal_alignment (in which case, preference is assigned directly to the valid candidate). It also is NEVER used to penalize accurate, confident claims for lack of hedging — only when ambiguity is objectively present and not assumed. When both candidates are visually grounded, multimodal-aligned, and contain claims affected by ambiguity, preference is given to the answer that: (a) explicitly acknowledges the ambiguity with non-hallucinatory language (e.g., ‘partially obscured’, ‘unclear due to shadow’, ‘possibly [object]’), and (b) avoids overclaiming or introducing unsupported details — even if cautious. The criterion does NOT penalize: (1) accurate, confident claims about unambiguous visual content, (2) non-hallucinated contextual or semantic inferences grounded in visual evidence, or (3) interpretive or aesthetic claims (e.g., ‘artistic rendering’, ‘mood’) — as long as they do not misrepresent visual content. It also does NOT evaluate: (1) object identity mislabeling if visually supported, (2) spatial relationships (evaluated under visual_coherence), or (3) non-visual factual claims (evaluated under multimodal_alignment). Hallucinated claims — even with ‘possibly’ or ‘appears to be’ — are always disqualified under multimodal_alignment — and this criterion must not be invoked to override that disqualification. The criterion must explicitly state: ‘If visual evidence is unambiguous (even if the answer is factually incorrect), this criterion is inapplicable — defer to visual_grounding or multimodal_alignment.’ Workers must verify ambiguity is objectively present before applying — not assume it from absence of detail or description. ‘Possibly’ is only acceptable if it qualifies a claim that is visually supported — not a fabricated claim (e.g., ‘possibly holding a frisbee’ when no frisbee is visible). The criterion must explicitly prohibit using cautious phrasing to mask hallucinations or factual misstatements — which are disqualifying under multimodal_alignment. It must also emphasize that ambiguity resolution is only valid if the claim is visually grounded — and must never be used to override visual_grounding or multimodal_alignment. If both candidates are equally accurate in handling ambiguity, preference must defer to other criteria — never to this criterion. The criterion must include an explicit example: ‘If Candidate A says “a cat sitting” (clearly visible) and Candidate B says “possibly a dog, legs obscured” (ambiguous visual evidence), Candidate A is preferred — ambiguity resolution is not invoked because Candidate B’s claim is not factually grounded or visually unambiguous. If Candidate A is hallucinated (e.g., ‘a flying cat’) and Candidate B is grounded, Candidate B is preferred — ambiguity resolution is not invoked.’

all_criteria.name: visual_grounding
all_criteria.description: The answer must accurately reflect what is visible in the image — describing elements, positions, colors, textures, or actions that can be directly observed. An answer is preferred if it avoids speculation or assumes unseen elements.

all_criteria.name: question_relevance
all_criteria.description: The answer must directly address the question without drifting into irrelevant topics. It should match the question’s intent — e.g., if the question asks about arrangement, the answer should focus on spatial or compositional details, not background stories or unrelated facts.

all_criteria.name: factual_consistency
all_criteria.description: The answer must be factually consistent with the visual evidence. If the image shows a cat, it should not be described as a dog. If an object is partially visible, it should not be claimed to be fully present or absent.

all_criteria.name: avoidance_of_hallucination
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer introduces any false, fabricated, or unsupported visual details not present in the image — including objects, attributes, actions, or spatial relationships. Hallucinations are penalized even if they appear plausible or are common in real life. Evaluation is done by cross-checking every claim in the answer against the visual evidence. For example, claiming ‘a red umbrella is being held by the person’ when no umbrella is visible is a hallucination. This criterion applies to all answers, regardless of question type, and is inapplicable when the answer is purely interpretive or metaphorical (e.g., ‘the scene feels hopeful’) — but only if such interpretations are visually grounded. Accuracy is measured by whether hallucinated content is absent or explicitly flagged as uncertain.

all_criteria.name: completeness
all_criteria.description: Completeness evaluates whether an answer includes all visually verifiable and semantically relevant elements necessary to fully answer the question — without hallucinating, fabricating, or adding unsupported details. An answer is preferred if it covers all visible components directly tied to the question’s intent (e.g., object identity, position, action, or interaction), even if minor or nuanced (e.g., posture, direction, or background context). It is NOT rewarded for verbosity, speculative inference, or background details unless they are visually grounded and semantically relevant. Completeness is evaluated ONLY after visual grounding and factual consistency are confirmed — hallucinated or factually incorrect content automatically disqualifies an answer, regardless of coverage. It is inapplicable when the question is meta, abstract, or does not require visual description. Omitting a clearly visible, question-relevant element (e.g., a person’s action in a question about movement) is a failure of completeness, but omitting non-essential or ambiguous elements (e.g., background texture) is not penalized. Workers must prioritize accuracy over coverage and flag cases of visual ambiguity by using calibrated uncertainty rather than fabricating details. Completeness rewards contextually reasonable inferences (e.g., inferring ‘clean and professional’ from white attire) as long as they are visually supported — but penalizes hallucinations (e.g., adding a nonexistent object or misrepresenting motion) even if they seem plausible or ‘more complete’. Examples: ‘a woman sitting at a desk’ is complete; ‘a woman sitting at a desk, wearing a hat’ is complete if the hat is visible; ‘a woman sitting at a desk, wearing a hat and holding a sword’ is incomplete if the sword is hallucinated. Always defer to visual evidence: if an element is not visible, its omission is not a failure of completeness — its addition is a hallucination. Completeness does not penalize interpretive or aesthetic language grounded in visual cues — e.g., ‘layered composition’ or ‘balanced framing’ — as long as they are contextually plausible and visually supported. Finally, completeness is not about quantity or exhaustiveness — it’s about faithful, relevant coverage of what is visible, and is strictly secondary to visual grounding and factual consistency.

all_criteria.name: specificity
all_criteria.description: The answer should provide precise, detailed, and concrete descriptions — e.g., specifying ‘left eye’ rather than ‘eye’, or ‘blood near mouth’ rather than ‘blood on face’. Vague or general statements are less preferred.

all_criteria.name: calibrated_uncertainty
all_criteria.description: When the visual evidence is ambiguous or incomplete, the answer should acknowledge uncertainty — e.g., ‘possibly’, ‘likely’, or ‘not clearly visible’ — rather than asserting certainty. Overconfidence in unsupported claims reduces quality.

all_criteria.name: clear_language
all_criteria.description: The answer should be grammatically correct, easy to understand, and free of unnecessary jargon or ambiguity. Clarity enhances accessibility and ensures the human evaluator can quickly assess the quality without confusion.

all_criteria.name: coherence_and_structure
all_criteria.description: The answer should be logically organized — with clear transitions, consistent terminology, and a logical flow — so the viewer can follow the description without mental effort. Disorganized or contradictory phrasing reduces credibility.

all_criteria.name: biological_or_realistic_plausibility
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer’s description of a living being (human or animal) is anatomically accurate or behaviorally consistent with known biological facts — e.g., a dog sniffing the ground is plausible; a dog flying is not. It applies ONLY when: (1) the visual evidence clearly identifies a living being (e.g., visible anatomy, posture, motion, or species-typical features), and (2) the answer describes its anatomy, posture, motion, or species-typical behavior — NOT emotional states, social roles, clothing, spatial context (unless it implies biological action like ‘leaning to pick up an object’), or quantitative/spatial claims (e.g., ‘left of’, ‘two meters away’). It is inapplicable to: (1) inanimate objects, logos, furniture, or background elements; (2) facial expressions, emotional states, or personality traits (e.g., ‘happy’, ‘serious’, ‘arrogant’); (3) inferred or speculative claims not visually supported — even if biologically plausible (e.g., ‘a cat flying’); (4) claims about non-visible objects (e.g., ‘holding a frisbee’) — which are hallucinations and must be evaluated under ‘avoidance_of_hallucination’ or ‘multimodal_alignment’. Biological plausibility is assessed ONLY AFTER visual grounding and factual consistency are confirmed — if an answer is visually ungrounded or factually incorrect, this criterion is inapplicable and must NOT be used to override other criteria. Hallucinated details — even if biologically plausible — are penalized under ‘avoidance_of_hallucination’ and must never be evaluated here. When applicable, the answer must not hallucinate anatomical impossibilities or species-specific behavioral violations (e.g., a cat riding a bicycle, a human with extra limbs). If two answers are equally visually grounded and factually correct, biological plausibility may be used as a tiebreaker — ONLY if both are equally grounded and both avoid hallucinations — and only if the claim is visually supported. Spatial relationships (e.g., ‘behind’, ‘in front of’) are evaluated under ‘visual_coherence’ or ‘completeness’ — not under biological plausibility — and any misalignment invalidates the answer regardless of biological accuracy. This criterion is strictly secondary — it never overrides visual grounding or factual consistency, and must never be used as a default preference or tiebreaker unless explicitly applicable. Workers must explicitly note inapplicability when the subject is not a living being or when visual evidence is insufficient — and must defer to other criteria (especially ‘visual_grounding’ and ‘avoidance_of_hallucination’) in such cases. Examples: ‘a cat arching its back in fear’ is applicable; ‘a person wearing a hat’ is inapplicable unless the hat implies biological behavior (e.g., ‘wearing a hat to keep warm’); ‘a dog sniffing the ground’ is applicable; ‘a dog flying’ is hallucinated — penalized under ‘avoidance_of_hallucination’. Workers must NOT use this criterion to evaluate non-living objects, emotional states, spatial relationships, or inferred actions — even if those claims are biologically plausible. If visual evidence contradicts a biological claim, the visually accurate answer is preferred — even if it is less biologically plausible. Biological plausibility is not evaluated for static poses (e.g., ‘sitting’) unless they imply motion or abnormal anatomy — and posture claims are only evaluated if they involve biological behavior. Workers must prioritize visual grounding, factual consistency, and hallucination avoidance — biological plausibility is only for anatomical or behavioral claims that are visually supported and not hallucinated.

all_criteria.name: logical_consistency
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer contains any internal contradictions — i.e., conflicting claims about the same entity, state, or action — within its own text. It applies ONLY to semantic or temporal inconsistencies that arise from the answer’s own wording, such as: 'The person is both sitting and standing', 'The object is both visible and invisible', or 'The door is open and closed'. It does NOT evaluate: (1) factual accuracy against the visual image (handled by visual_grounding), (2) external real-world plausibility (handled by biological_or_realistic_plausibility), (3) interpretive ambiguity or stylistic vagueness (handled by specificity or visual_grounding), or (4) hallucinations or unsupported claims — unless they create internal contradictions. If an answer contains no internal contradictions, it is considered logically consistent and should not be penalized, even if it is factually wrong or visually ungrounded. When comparing two answers that are both logically consistent, preference should be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual_grounding, factual consistency, or completeness). This criterion is inapplicable if the answer contains no claims, is empty, or is entirely hallucinated without self-contradiction — in which case, the worker should evaluate other criteria or flag ambiguity. Workers must strictly avoid conflating logical consistency with visual accuracy or factual truth — internal coherence alone is sufficient to satisfy this criterion.

all_criteria.name: multimodal_alignment
all_criteria.description: The answer must align with the visual modality — for example, describing objects that are clearly visible, not relying on auditory or textual context that isn’t supported by the image. Evaluated by cross-checking visual evidence with textual claims.

all_criteria.name: action_or_state_accuracy
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer correctly identifies or infers a dynamic state or action (e.g., walking, running, opening, closing, jumping) based on visual cues — motion blur, posture, object position, or implied temporal change — and must be inapplicable if the question does not involve such inference. It does not apply to static object identification, spatial layout, text reading, or compositional descriptions unless they are directly tied to motion or state change (e.g., 'leaning into a turn' is valid; 'in a line' is not). Visual evidence must be clear and unambiguous for a definitive claim; if ambiguous, the answer must express calibrated uncertainty (e.g., 'possibly walking', 'not clearly open') rather than making a speculative inference. Hallucinated or unsupported state/action claims (e.g., 'the cat is dancing', 'the door is closing because of wind') are penalized. The criterion is only triggered when the question explicitly asks about motion, state change, or temporal indicators (e.g., 'Is the person running?', 'Is the door open?', 'What is the person doing?'). For static states (e.g., 'standing', 'wearing a hat'), the criterion does not apply — such descriptions are evaluated under visual grounding or specificity. Workers must first determine if the question is action/state-oriented before applying this criterion. Accuracy is measured solely on whether the inferred state/action matches visual evidence — not on detail level, aesthetic quality, or contextual plausibility. When tied, defer to other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, factual consistency).

all_criteria.name: contextual_sensitivity
all_criteria.description: The answer should respect the contextual setting of the image — e.g., recognizing indoor vs. outdoor, formal vs. casual, or cultural cues — and tailor its response accordingly. Evaluated by assessing whether the answer ignores or misinterprets contextual clues.

all_criteria.name: temporal_coherence
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer’s description of motion, dynamic action, or implied temporal sequence (e.g., ‘jumping’, ‘falling’, ‘opening’, ‘running’) is visually consistent with explicit or inferable motion cues — including motion blur, directional posture, trajectory lines, implied speed from posture or spacing, or dynamic body orientation — but ONLY when such cues are present and unambiguous. It applies exclusively to motion-related claims and does NOT apply to static postures (e.g., ‘sitting’, ‘standing’, ‘leaning’), object identity, presence, or structural descriptions (e.g., ‘on a curved track’, ‘in a tunnel’), which are evaluated under visual grounding or specificity. The criterion is INAPPLICABLE if motion cues are absent, ambiguous, or inferred from static posture (e.g., ‘leaning into a turn’ without visual motion) — workers must explicitly flag inapplicability and MUST defer to other criteria (visual grounding, multimodal alignment, specificity) to break ties or determine preference. This criterion is strictly secondary and NEVER overrides visual grounding or multimodal alignment — any answer that is visually ungrounded or factually inconsistent is disqualified under those criteria, and temporal_coherence is irrelevant. If one answer is disqualified under visual grounding or multimodal alignment, the other is preferred by default — even if temporal_coherence is inapplicable. Inapplicability does NOT imply preference — it simply means this criterion cannot resolve the comparison. Preference must be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, specificity, multimodal alignment) when temporal_coherence is inapplicable. When applicable, answers must not contradict visual evidence (e.g., claiming ‘landing’ when the person is airborne), and speculative inferences (e.g., ‘possibly falling’) are acceptable ONLY if grounded in motion cues — not if they contradict them. The criterion is NOT about factual plausibility (e.g., whether ‘browsing’ is physically possible) or structural accuracy (e.g., ‘ramp’, ‘bowl’), which are evaluated under visual grounding or factual consistency. Temporal_coherence must NEVER be used as a tiebreaker or preference guide when inapplicable — workers must strictly defer to other criteria. If both answers are temporally consistent, the criterion is inapplicable and preference is determined by other criteria. Workers must never assume preference based on temporal_coherence’s inapplicability — preference must be determined by visual grounding, specificity, or multimodal alignment. Preference derived from this criterion is ONLY valid if the criterion is applicable and both answers are equally valid — which is rare. Any preference based on this criterion is invalid unless motion cues are clearly present and both answers are temporally consistent. Workers must explicitly note ‘inapplicable’ when motion cues are absent or ambiguous — and must NOT infer motion from static posture, compositional context, or structural features. This criterion must never override visual grounding or factual consistency — even if one answer is more accurate, the visually grounded or factually correct answer must be preferred if temporal_coherence is inapplicable. Workers must not use this criterion to resolve preference between candidates with different structural or compositional descriptions — such comparisons must be handled by visual grounding or specificity. Workers must not penalize an answer for describing motion in a way that is visually consistent — even if it differs from another answer’s structural description — and must defer to other criteria if motion is not the focus or if structural accuracy is in question. Internal contradictions (e.g., ‘no ham’ while listing ‘Iberian ham’) are handled under multimodal_consistency, not temporal_coherence — and workers should never use temporal_coherence to resolve factual contradictions. Motion claims must be both visually supported and contextually accurate — not just visually supported — and any motion claim that contradicts other visual facts (e.g., ‘the door is open’ while the person is holding it shut) must be penalized under multimodal_alignment or visual_coherence, not temporal_coherence. Temporal_coherence is for evaluating motion consistency — not for resolving preference between disqualifying answers — and workers must not use it to justify disqualifying answers — even if the criterion is inapplicable — and must defer to visual grounding, specificity, or multimodal_alignment to resolve preference.

all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer’s explicit spatial relationship claims — defined as assertions using terms like 'left of', 'behind', 'in front of', 'overlapping', 'centered relative to', 'slightly closer', 'relatively far apart', 'on', 'under', 'above', 'beneath', 'beside', or 'within' — are factually consistent with the visual layout and relative positioning of at least two visually confirmed objects in the image. When both answers pass multimodal_alignment and both contain spatial claims, visual_coherence is used as a tiebreaker — preference is given to the answer with fewer or no factual misrepresentations of spatial relationships — but only if the claims are explicitly and visually verifiable. Spatial claims must not be hallucinated or misidentified — such claims are disqualifying under multimodal_alignment, not under visual_coherence. Workers must evaluate multimodal_alignment first — if one fails, visual_coherence is not considered — and preference is assigned directly by multimodal_alignment. Workers must never assume or introduce tiebreakers — especially arbitrary ones — when visual_coherence is inapplicable. If both answers are inapplicable (e.g., neither contains a spatial claim), preference must not be assigned — the pair should be marked as a tie or deferred to other criteria — without defaulting to a tiebreaker. The worker must not evaluate or reason about visual_coherence if either answer fails multimodal_alignment — and must immediately defer to multimodal_alignment or other criteria — without any ambiguity or room for interpretation. If both answers are invalid (e.g., both hallucinated), preference must not be assigned — the pair should be marked as a tie or deferred to other criteria — and workers must never assume or introduce tiebreakers. Finally, the criterion must explicitly state: (a) visual_coherence is never used to assign preference when one candidate fails multimodal_alignment — preference is determined solely by multimodal_alignment, (b) it is only a tiebreaker between two equally multimodal-aligned answers with spatial claims, (c) it is never used to justify preference for an invalid candidate, (d) spatial claims are mandatory for evaluation — no claim about visual representation (e.g., ‘smoke rising’) is evaluated under visual_coherence unless it is a spatial claim, (e) spatial accuracy is only evaluated if both candidates are multimodal-aligned — and (f) if neither candidate contains a spatial claim, preference must not be assigned — the pair must be marked as a tie or deferred to other criteria — without defaulting to a tiebreaker.

all_criteria.name: stylistic_clarity
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer uses clear, unambiguous, and grammatically correct language that minimizes interpretive ambiguity or stylistic vagueness — such as avoiding overly poetic, metaphorical, or emotionally charged expressions unless they are explicitly grounded in visual cues. It applies when the answer’s phrasing could confuse or mislead the reader (e.g., ‘mysterious glowing orb’ vs. ‘a red lightbulb’), or when stylistic choices obscure factual content. It is inapplicable if the language is purely descriptive, factual, or visually grounded — and does not override visual grounding or factual consistency. For example, ‘the cat is staring intensely’ is acceptable if the visual evidence supports intensity, but ‘the cat is a mystical guardian’ is penalized for stylistic overreach. Workers must distinguish between stylistic enhancement and hallucination — if a metaphor is visually supported (e.g., ‘balanced composition’ in a symmetrical image), it is acceptable. This criterion is not about aesthetic quality or interpretive depth — only whether language is clear and unambiguous for the given question. Preference is given to the answer with the clearest, most direct phrasing — even if less stylistically rich — as long as it remains visually grounded. It is strictly secondary to visual grounding and factual consistency — if either is violated, this criterion is inapplicable.

all_criteria.name: semantic_specificity
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates the degree to which an answer includes verifiably accurate, contextually relevant visual attributes (e.g., color, shape, posture, material, identity, position) that are directly supported by the image — without introducing hallucinations, inferred claims, or aesthetic/interpretive language. Specificity is measured by the quantity and quality of such attributes, but only when both candidate answers are visually grounded and factually consistent (i.e., no hallucinations or misidentifications under multimodal_alignment). Higher specificity is preferred only as a tiebreaker when both answers are equally valid — never as a primary evaluation tool. Workers must first verify visual grounding and factual accuracy using multimodal_alignment before applying this criterion. If visual evidence is ambiguous or insufficient to support a claim (including count or detail), workers must use calibrated uncertainty (e.g., ‘possibly’, ‘appears to be’) — and the criterion is inapplicable. Specificity is not rewarded for: (1) non-visual or semantic claims (e.g., ‘browsing Apple pages’), (2) aesthetic or evaluative terms (e.g., ‘striking’, ‘balanced’, ‘messy’), (3) inferred structural or compositional claims (e.g., ‘sandwich’, ‘arranged between’) unless visually implied by occlusion, posture, or alignment, (4) speculative or hypothetical details (e.g., ‘a blue ribbon’ when the ribbon is green), or (5) claims that misrepresent visual structure (e.g., calling a logo ‘human-shaped’ when it is text-based — unless that description is accurate and literal). Attributes must be literal, observable, and not stylistic — e.g., ‘a black Labrador sitting on a wooden floor’ is more specific than ‘a dog sitting on the floor’ — if both are visually grounded and factually correct. Specificity must not override visual grounding or factual consistency — if either is violated, the criterion is inapplicable and must not be used to justify preference. Workers must explicitly flag inapplicability if either answer is factually incorrect, visually ungrounded, or if visual evidence is insufficient. The criterion is inapplicable if one answer is invalid under multimodal_alignment — preference must be determined by other criteria. When evaluating specificity, workers must prioritize visual fidelity over textual quantity — e.g., ‘a person leaning forward with hands on hips’ is more specific than ‘a person standing’ — if both are visually grounded and factually correct, and the former accurately reflects posture. Workers must never penalize an answer for omitting details that are not visually confirmed — and must avoid subjective judgments like ‘unnecessary complexity’ or ‘misleading’ — which are not allowed under this criterion. Specificity is only a tiebreaker — it does not determine preference if one answer is visually ungrounded, factually incorrect, or hallucinated. In cases of visual ambiguity (e.g., abstract art or occluded objects), the default preference should be for the answer that avoids overclaiming or introducing unsupported structure — not the one that adds more speculative detail. Workers must explicitly note ‘inapplicable’ when the criterion’s conditions are not met — and must not infer specificity from stylistic or interpretive claims. This criterion is strictly secondary — never used to override visual grounding, factual consistency, or multimodal_alignment. Workers must prioritize literal visual evidence — not semantic inference — and must reject any answer that contains even one hallucinated or unsupported attribute — regardless of how ‘specific’ it sounds. Specificity is measured only on verifiable, core descriptive elements (object identity, posture, spatial positioning) — not on peripheral or ambiguous details — and must not be used to justify preference between answers where one is visually ungrounded or factually incorrect. The criterion is inapplicable if either candidate is visually ungrounded or factually incorrect — and preference must be determined by other criteria. Workers must never use this criterion to evaluate aesthetic or interpretive claims — even if they appear contextually relevant — and must defer to other criteria if visual evidence is insufficient or ambiguous.

all_criteria.name: contextual_fidelity
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer’s description respects the visual context and narrative implied by the image — such as background, lighting, environment, or implied interaction — without fabricating or misrepresenting contextually relevant elements. It applies when the answer includes contextual details (e.g., ‘indoor’, ‘daylight’, ‘on a street’, ‘with a crowd’) that are either visually evident or logically implied by the image’s composition — and penalizes answers that ignore or contradict contextual cues (e.g., describing a night scene as ‘brightly lit’ or an indoor scene as ‘outdoor’). It is inapplicable if the image lacks sufficient contextual cues (e.g., abstract art, heavily blurred scenes) — in which case, calibrated uncertainty must be used. Contextual fidelity is evaluated by comparing how accurately each answer reflects the image’s setting, lighting, or implied environment — preference is given to the answer that aligns with the visual context, even if it is less specific or more general. It does not override visual grounding or factual consistency — if an answer is factually incorrect or visually ungrounded, contextual fidelity is irrelevant. Workers must explicitly note inapplicability when the visual context is ambiguous or insufficient — and must not use this criterion to justify preferring an answer that ignores visual context. This criterion is not about aesthetic interpretation or stylistic enhancement — only whether the answer’s context is visually or logically consistent with the image’s environment. Example: ‘a person walking in bright daylight’ is contextually faithful if the image shows sunlight — ‘a person walking at night’ is contextually faithful if the image shows dark lighting — but ‘a person walking in a desert’ is contextually faithful only if the image shows desert features.

all_criteria.name: calibrated_uncertainty_usage
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer appropriately uses calibrated uncertainty (e.g., ‘possibly’, ‘likely’, ‘appears to be’, ‘unclear’) when the visual evidence is ambiguous, incomplete, or insufficient to make a definitive claim. It applies only when the image lacks clear visual support for a specific assertion — such as occlusion, low resolution, or ambiguous object identity. It penalizes answers that overstate certainty (e.g., ‘definitely a dog’ when the object is partially obscured) and rewards those that reflect uncertainty appropriately (e.g., ‘possibly a dog’, ‘unclear whether it’s a dog or a cat’). It is inapplicable when the visual evidence is unambiguous — in which case, the answer must be specific and confident. It does not override visual grounding or factual consistency — if an answer is factually incorrect or visually ungrounded, this criterion is irrelevant. The criterion is strictly secondary — it only evaluates the appropriateness of uncertainty phrasing, not the truth of the claim. Accuracy is measured by whether the uncertainty level matches the visual ambiguity — higher accuracy is given to answers that use uncertainty precisely and avoid overconfidence. This criterion is not about stylistic tone or interpretive depth — only whether uncertainty is calibrated to the visual evidence.

all_criteria.name: multimodal_consistency
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer’s language is internally consistent with the visual evidence — meaning the answer does not contradict itself or imply conflicting visual states (e.g., claiming ‘the door is open’ while also stating ‘the door is locked’), or misaligns with the visual context (e.g., describing ‘a person walking’ while the visual shows ‘a person standing still’). It applies to all visual descriptions and must be evaluated independently of factual correctness or biological plausibility — even if the answer is factually wrong, it may still be multimodally consistent if it does not contradict itself or misrepresent the visual state. It is inapplicable if the answer contains no claims, is empty, or is entirely hallucinated — in which case, it must be evaluated under multimodal_alignment or avoidance_of_hallucination. The criterion is not about semantic or contextual coherence — only whether the visual claims are logically consistent with each other and with the image. Preference is given to the answer that is internally consistent — even if both are hallucinated — as long as one does not contradict the other. Workers must evaluate internal consistency first, then defer to visual grounding or factual consistency if a contradiction is present. Accuracy is measured by whether the answer’s claims are logically consistent with the visual evidence and with each other — not by truth or plausibility.

all_criteria.name: visual_ambiguity_resolution
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer explicitly acknowledges and appropriately resolves genuine visual ambiguities — defined as situations where visual evidence is objectively unclear due to occlusion, low resolution, lighting/shadow interference, motion blur, or partial visibility — without fabricating, hallucinating, or misrepresenting visual content. It applies ONLY when: (1) visual ambiguity is objectively present in the image (e.g., object partially hidden, structure obscured by shadow, fine detail indistinct due to resolution), and (2) the answer makes a visual claim that is directly affected by that ambiguity. If either condition is not met, the criterion is INAPPLICABLE — and preference must be determined by visual_grounding or multimodal_alignment first. The criterion is strictly secondary and NEVER overrides visual_grounding or multimodal_alignment — any answer that is visually ungrounded, factually incorrect, or contains hallucinations is disqualified under those criteria, regardless of ambiguity handling. Hallucinated claims — even if framed as ambiguity resolutions (e.g., ‘possibly a cat, but the legs are unclear’) — are invalid and must be disqualified under multimodal_alignment — this criterion does not evaluate hallucination. The criterion evaluates only how ambiguity is handled — not the factual accuracy of the claim — and penalizes only when the answer ignores or misrepresents the visual ambiguity (e.g., claiming ‘a dog’ when the image shows only partial legs under shadow, without acknowledging the uncertainty). It does NOT penalize: (1) accurate, confident claims about clearly visible content, (2) cautious phrasing (e.g., ‘possibly’, ‘appears to be’, ‘unclear’) — if used appropriately to acknowledge ambiguity, (3) non-hallucinated contextual or semantic inferences grounded in visual evidence, or (4) interpretive or aesthetic claims (e.g., ‘artistic rendering’, ‘mood’) — as long as they do not misrepresent visual content. It also does NOT evaluate: (1) object identity mislabeling (e.g., ‘can’ vs. ‘bottle’) if visually supported, (2) spatial or structural relationships (evaluated under visual_coherence), or (3) factual claims about non-visual attributes (evaluated under multimodal_alignment). When applicable, preference is given to the answer that acknowledges the visual ambiguity with appropriate, non-hallucinatory language — such as ‘partially obscured’, ‘unclear due to shadow’, or ‘possibly [object]’ — without introducing unsupported details or overclaiming. The criterion is exclusively a tiebreaker — only used when both answers are visually grounded, multimodal-aligned, and both contain visual claims affected by ambiguity — and must never be used to justify preference over an answer that is already disqualified under other criteria. Workers must first verify visual_grounding and multimodal_alignment for both candidates — and only evaluate ambiguity resolution if both pass — otherwise, the criterion is inapplicable. If both answers are equally accurate in handling ambiguity, preference must defer to other criteria (e.g., visual_grounding, specificity) — never to this criterion. Workers must flag the criterion as inapplicable if: (a) the visual evidence is unambiguous (e.g., object clearly identifiable and fully visible), (b) the answer makes no visual claim, or (c) the answer contains any hallucination or misrepresentation — even if framed as ambiguity resolution. Accuracy is measured by whether the answer acknowledges the visual ambiguity in a non-hallucinatory, contextually appropriate manner — without fabricating or misrepresenting visual content — and whether it avoids overconfident claims that contradict the visual evidence. The criterion must explicitly state: ‘If visual evidence is unambiguous, this criterion is inapplicable — defer to visual grounding or multimodal_alignment.’ Workers must not assume ambiguity exists for unconfirmed claims — only when visual evidence is genuinely ambiguous — and must not use caution (e.g., ‘possibly’) to mask factual inaccuracies — such claims are disqualified under multimodal_alignment. This criterion must never be used to resolve preference between hallucinated and grounded answers — hallucinated answers are always disqualified under multimodal_alignment — and the criterion must not be invoked to override that disqualification.

all_criteria.name: temporal_consistency
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer’s description of motion, state changes, or implied temporal progression is consistent with the static visual evidence — i.e., whether the answer implies a sequence, duration, or transition that cannot be supported by the image (e.g., claiming ‘the dog is running’ when the image shows a static pose, or ‘the person just opened the door’ when the door is closed). It applies ONLY when: (1) the answer includes a claim about motion, state change, or implied time sequence, and (2) the visual evidence is static (no motion blur, no temporal cues) — meaning no explicit or implicit indication of movement, action, or temporal progression is visible. It is INAPPLICABLE if: (a) the claim is not about motion or temporal sequence, (b) the visual evidence is dynamic (e.g., motion blur, action pose, temporal cues like a time stamp or multiple frames), or (c) the claim is hallucinated or factually incorrect — in which case, preference is determined by visual_grounding or multimodal_alignment first. The criterion does NOT evaluate: (1) static posture claims (e.g., ‘sitting’, ‘standing’ — handled by action_or_state_accuracy), (2) factual accuracy of object identity or spatial layout (handled by multimodal_alignment), (3) semantic or contextual inferences (e.g., ‘formal setting’), or (4) inferred motion without visual cues (e.g., ‘possibly moving’ — handled by action_or_state_accuracy). It does NOT penalize: (a) cautious phrasing (e.g., ‘appears to be’, ‘possibly’) — if used appropriately — (b) plausible inferences grounded in visual evidence, or (c) non-hallucinated additional context that does not misrepresent visual content. Preference is given to the answer that avoids implying motion or temporal progression not supported by visual evidence — such as claiming ‘the ball is rolling’ when the image shows a static ball. If both answers are visually grounded, multimodal-aligned, and factually correct, preference is given to the one with fewer or no claims implying unsupported temporal progression — but only if the claims are explicitly and visually verifiable. The criterion is strictly secondary to visual_grounding and multimodal_alignment — if an answer fails those, it is disqualified regardless of temporal consistency. Workers must first verify visual_grounding and multimodal_alignment — and only evaluate temporal_consistency for answers that pass those criteria. If both answers are equally accurate, defer to other criteria — never to subjective judgment. The criterion must not be used to penalize accurate, specific claims that do not require temporal evaluation — only when visual evidence supports a claim about motion or temporal progression. If the criterion is inapplicable for both answers (e.g., no motion or temporal claims), defer to other criteria — never to subjective judgment. Importantly, temporal_consistency cannot be used to evaluate or justify preference for hallucinated or misidentified claims — such answers are automatically disqualified under multimodal_alignment, and the other answer is preferred without invoking this criterion. If both answers are inapplicable, preference must not be assigned — the pair should be marked as a tie or deferred to other criteria without defaulting to a tiebreaker. Workers must never assume or introduce tiebreakers — especially arbitrary ones — when this criterion is inapplicable to both candidates. Preference is never given to an answer that contains hallucinated temporal claims — even if it is more specific — and this criterion is only used to break ties between equally grounded and factually correct answers. Workers must evaluate visual grounding and multimodal_alignment first — and factual consistency is only evaluated after those are verified — with temporal_consistency being strictly secondary to them. The criterion must emphasize that temporal claims are irrelevant if the answer is factually wrong — and must be evaluated only after visual grounding and multimodal_alignment are verified. Finally, the criterion must explicitly state that if both candidates are inapplicable, preference must not be assigned — either the pair should be marked as a tie or the worker should be instructed to defer to other criteria without defaulting to the first option. The criterion must also clarify that it is never valid to assume or introduce tiebreakers — especially arbitrary ones — when the criterion itself is inapplicable to both candidates. The criterion must also avoid duplication with existing criteria — such as action_or_state_accuracy (which evaluates motion/state in static or dynamic contexts) and visual_coherence (which evaluates spatial relationships, not temporal progression).
